title: TB4-12081
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXXXXX (the Appellant) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXX (the Appellant) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. She alleges to be a citizen of Nigeria and no other country. The Appellant has submitted new evidence in support of her appeal and requests an oral hearing. She asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute a positive determination or to refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.

This appeal is allowed. Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter back to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel. Background
The Appellant alleged before the RPD that, upon return to Nigeria, she will be harmed by her father and others because she refused to enter into a forced marriage.

The Appellant's application for refugee protection was heard on November 5, 2014. By a decision of November 12, 2014, the RPD rejected the claim. The RPD found that the Appellant failed to establish her identity on a balance of probabilities. It also found her testimony regarding being forced to marry a chief was lacking in credibility.
The Appellant submits that the RPD committed errors in assessing her evidence and rejecting her identity documents. ANALYSIS Role of the RAD

What is the role of the RAD in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD? The Appellant refers to Huruglica1 in her Memorandum. In Huruglica, the Court considered the appropriate relationship between the RAD and the RPD. It found that the RAD had erred in simply reviewing the RPD's decision on a standard of reasonableness, rather than conducting its own independent assessment of the Appellants' refugee claims. The Court held that the RAD's application of a reasonableness standard curtailed the tribunal's appellate role, contrary to the purpose of the RAD and the provisions of IRPA. In the Court's view, the RAD should not even engage in a standard of review analysis; rather, it should consider the purpose of the appellate tribunal, the statutory provisions, comparable expertise, and comparative appellate regimes.2

Justice Phelan stated the following in Huruglica: 54. Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.3 55. In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."4

The RAD will therefore review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of the Appellant's refugee claim, recognizing and respecting the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion. Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own determination. Admissibility of Evidence Submitted on Appeal

Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of her claim or that was not reasonably available, or that she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. It is for the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in her Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of Section 110(4) and how that evidence relates to her.5

The Appellant has tendered two documents as proposed new evidence in support of her appeal. The first document is a photocopy of two pages from a Federal Republic of Nigeria passport issued in the Appellant's name in Ottawa on XXX 2014.6 The second document is a letter from the Nigeria High Commission in Ottawa, dated December 4, 2014, authenticating the Appellant's Nigerian driver's license.7

The Appellant submits that the proposed new evidence was not reasonably available to her at the time of her hearing before the RPD because she did not have the money to travel to the Nigerian embassy in Ottawa or to pay to obtain a new passport. She indicates that she was able to travel to Ottawa to obtain the documents only after her church provided her with the funds. The Appellant submits that the proposed new evidence is relevant in resolving the issue of her identity.

The Appellant failed to indicate in her Memorandum why she was unable to obtain the funds to obtain her passport and authentication of her Nigerian driver's license prior to the rejection of the claim. Nonetheless, the documents are dated subsequent to the rejection of the claim by the RPD and would assist the Appellant in establishing her identity. Since they arose after the rejection of the Appellant's claim and are highly relevant to the issue of her identity they will be accepted as new evidence in this appeal.8 Application for an Oral Hearing
The Appellant asks that an oral hearing be held, pursuant to Section 110(6) of IRPA and RAD Rule 3(3)(d).9

Section 110(3) of IRPA requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the Appellant. The person who is the subject of the appeal may, pursuant to Section 110(4), present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

According to Section 110(6), upon which the Appellant relies, the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. In this appeal, where there is no evidence from or in response to the Minister, the documentary evidence referred to in Section 110(3) must be understood in relation to Section 110(4).

When read together, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new (Section 110(4)) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

The RAD has reviewed the new evidence admitted in this appeal. It notes that the new evidence assists in establishing the Appellant's identity. However, neither of the documents entered as new evidence place the Appellant in Nigeria at the time of the alleged incidents that purportedly caused the Appellant to flee Nigeria in 2014. The Appellant's passport contains no information regarding her departure from Nigeria. The authentication of her Nigerian driver's license indicates that her driver's license expired on July 14, 2012, over two years before she allegedly fled Nigeria, and also does not place the Appellant in Nigeria at the time of the alleged incidents.

The RAD finds that the new evidence does not justify allowing the Appellant's refugee protection claim. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing and the Appellant's request for an oral hearing is denied. The RPD's Findings

Effort to obtain new Nigerian passport - The RPD drew a negative inference from the Appellant not presenting a Nigerian passport as an identity document prior to her hearing. It noted that the Appellant made no attempt to obtain a new Nigerian passport after the passport she used to travel to the United States was taken by her agent.

As noted above, the Appellant submits that, at the time of her hearing before the RPD, she did not have the money to travel to the Nigerian embassy in Ottawa or the money to pay to obtain a new passport. She indicates that she was able to travel to Ottawa to obtain the passport only after her church provided her with the funds. The Appellant argues that she was not asked by the RPD why she had failed to obtain a new passport in Canada.
The RAD notes that the Appellant was asked by the RPD at her hearing why she had not tried to replace her Nigerian passport. The Appellant indicated that she was not settled yet.

The RAD notes that the Appellant submitted her certificate of birth,10 her Nigerian driver's license11 and a school certificate12 as identity evidence prior to and on the day of her hearing before the RPD. The Appellant had been in Canada for approximately three months prior to her hearing. The Appellant's explanation for not having replaced her Nigerian passport prior to her hearing was reasonable. She had been in Canada for a short period of time and had presented documents intended to establish her identity. As such, the RAD does not concur with the RPD drawing a negative inference from the Appellant not presenting a Nigerian passport as an identity document prior to her hearing.

Weight assigned to school certificate - The RPD placed no weight on the Appellant's school certificate as evidence of her identity. It noted problems with the document. One problem noted was that the facial image in the photograph affixed to the certificate was not discernable and the RPD was unable to ascertain if the person in the photograph was the Appellant. It also noted that the word "COPY" appeared throughout a section of the certificate.

The Appellant submits that the RPD had no sufficient reasons to reject her school certificate and committed errors by failing to give her the benefit of the doubt. She notes that the certificate was issued a long time ago (2004).

The RAD notes that the Appellant's year of birth on her school certificate13 differs from her year of birth on her birth certificate.14 However, the RPD did not address this discrepancy with the Appellant. The issues the RPD had with the school certificate, although noteworthy, are not sufficient to discredit the certificate entirely, without further analysis. As such the RAD does not concur with the RPD that the certificate holds no weight in establishing the Appellant's identity.

Explanation for obtaining driver's license - The RPD found that the Appellant's reasons for obtaining a driver's license in Nigeria unreasonable and illogical. It noted that the Appellant alleged she obtained her driver's license solely for the purpose of establishing her identity in Nigeria (for banking and other activities) and not to drive. The Appellant indicated to the RPD that, at the time she obtained her driver's license, she did not have her passport yet and her National Identity Card (NIC) had expired. She also indicated that the NIC expired annually. The RPD noted documentary evidence indicating that NICs are issued for 10 years. It also noted that taking driving lessons, simply in order to obtain a driver's license for the purposes of establishing her identity for government and other related business in Nigeria, is unreasonable given there exists an identity card issued to all Nigerians for this stated purpose. The RPD found the Appellant's explanation regarding her driver's license lacking in credibility. The RPD also noted the prevalence of false documents in Nigeria.

The Appellant submits that there was no evidence before the RPD that Nigerians cannot obtain a driver's license for the sole purpose of identity. It was also submitted that the RPD erred by assuming that all documents from Nigeria are fraudulent. The Appellant noted that none of her identity documents were issued in Benin City where documentary evidence indicates that documents could be procured.

The RAD notes that the Appellant's driver's licence would have been valid for less time than a NIC; five years compared to ten years. The Appellant's assertion that NICs are valid for one year when the documentary evidence indicates that they are valid for ten years undermines her credibility. It would be reasonable to expect her to know how many years a NIC is valid for since she is an educated woman who alleges she was in possession of a NIC. Furthermore, she alleges she gave consideration to renewing her NIC before she sought another form of photo identification with a driver's license.

While the RPD found that the Appellant's reasons for obtaining a driver's license in Nigeria unreasonable, illogical and lacking in credibility, it failed to actually consider the document itself. The national driver's licence15 has the Appellant's name and photograph and appears to have security features, including background printing and a bar code. The RPD could have compared this licence to a sample that was in evidence before it,16 but it does not seem to have done so. It is unclear from the RPD's reasons why this document does not assist the Appellant in establishing her identity.

As such, the RAD concurs with the RPD that the Appellant's reasons for obtaining a driver's license lacks credibility. The RAD finds that the Appellant's lack of knowledge about the validity period of a NIC, when it would be reasonable to expect her to know this undermines her credibility. However, the RAD does not concur with the RPD in dismissing the Appellant's Nigerian driver's license, as an identity document, altogether.

Birth Certificate - The RPD noted that the Appellant's birth certificate was issued in 1996, when she was born in 1989. The Appellant indicated to the RPD that she did not know why it was issued in 1996 and did not know the whereabouts of her original birth certificate. The RPD found the Appellant's explanations for the date on her birth certificate were not reasonably explained.

The RAD does not concur with the RPD's finding regarding the birth certificate. The RPD indicates that the Appellant's explanations were not reasonable but fails to indicate why they were not reasonable. The RPD is required to explain the reasons for their findings. Without reasons, it is difficult for the RAD to recognize and respect this credibility finding.

Boyfriend's beating - The Appellant alleges that in January 2014, after visiting her boyfriend, her father, the chief she was to marry and four thugs attacked her boyfriend. She testified at her hearing before the RPD that her boyfriend was punched and dragged for approximately 30 minutes by the four thugs and she witnessed the attack. She also indicated that her boyfriend did not need medical attention, nor was he bleeding, but had bruises on his jaw. The RPD found the Appellant's account of the beating lacking in credibility. It noted that it was unreasonable and incredible that four men could beat and drag another man for 30 minutes and the victim not require medical attention or the beating did not result in any bleeding.

The Appellant submits that she did not contradict her claim when she testified that her boyfriend was not injured but sustained only bruises after he was beaten by four thugs for about 30 minutes. She argues that she said 30 minutes because that was an approximate amount of time and was not the actual time of the beating because she did not record or time the event. The Appellant submits that the RPD committed an error in perversely impugning her credibility and evidence by assuming that every beating that involved slapping and kicking would always result in hospitalization.

The RAD concurs with the RPD's finding that the Appellant's account of the beating of her boyfriend lacked credibility. The Appellant testified before the RPD that her boyfriend was beaten, punched, kicked and dragged on the street by four men for approximately 30 minutes. It is absurd for the Appellant to suggest that her boyfriend suffered no injuries except bruising after being brutally attacked by four men for approximately 30 minutes. It would be reasonable to expect the victim of such an attack to require medical treatment for injuries sustained in the attack. It would also be reasonable to expect the victim of such an attack to suffer lacerations and experience bleeding. The Appellant's assertion that her boyfriend only had bruising on his face and jaw, when such an attack would likely cause more serious injuries, further undermines the Appellant's credibility.

Returning home after sneaking out to visit boyfriend - The Appellant alleges that, following the incident when her boyfriend was beaten, she was forced to return home and held against her will for two days. She testified before the RPD that she managed to sneak out of her home on the third day to see her boyfriend and returned home afterwards. When asked by the RPD why she returned home after visiting her boyfriend, the Appellant indicated that she did not believe her father was serious about the marriage. When asked why she believed her father was not serious about the marriage, considering that she had witnessed the beating of her boyfriend with the chief present and was held against her will, the Appellant indicated that it was because a wedding date had not been set. The RPD found the Appellant's explanation for returning to her family home, after all that had transpired, unreasonable and lacking in credibility.

In assessing the Appellant's actions, the RPD noted that it considered the Gender Guidelines.17 It noted that the Appellant had indicated her refusal to marry the Chief and had witnessed violence directed towards her and her boyfriend. It found that it was unreasonable, when the Appellant had an opportunity to sneak out of the home and did so, that she would return home simply because a marriage date had not been set. It further found the Appellant's account of the event lacking in credibility as she had an opportunity to leave and chose to return to the family home where she had just escaped being held captive. The RPD concluded that the Appellant's allegation of the threat of having to marry a chief was lacking in credibility.

The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to properly apply the Gender Guidelines to her claim. She argues that the RPD wrongly concluded that the Gender Guidelines require a young woman, such as her, fleeing forced marriage to immediately flee at the first opportunity. The Appellant submits that it was her boyfriend who finally encouraged her to flee her home and go to Lagos to hide with her aunt. She argues that the RPD failed to consider the evidence that she was unemployed, was dependant on her parents for support and the difficulty she would face if she had decided to flee to a new location where she would have nobody to depend on for support.

The RAD notes that, while the RPD made reference to the Gender Guidelines, it provided no analysis in relation to the Gender Guidelines. The Gender Guidelines indicate that, in determining the reasonableness of a woman's recourse to an internal flight alternative (IFA), decision-makers should consider the ability of women, because of their gender, to travel safely to the IFA and to stay there without facing undue hardship. It is further noted in the Gender Guidelines that in determining the reasonableness of an IFA, the decision-makers should take into account factors including religious, economic, and cultural factors, and consider whether and how these factors affect women in the IFA. Although IFA was not a determinative issue in the RPD decision, its analysis of the Appellant's action of returning home after escaping would justify assessing her action under this area of the Gender Guidelines as it questions the Appellant's reasons for not fleeing the family home to an alternate location at a particular time. The RPD's findings in this area are not supported by the Gender Guidelines. It failed to address the Appellant's circumstances and the reasonableness of fleeing when she initially escaped her home. As such, the RAD does not concur with the RPD finding that the Appellant's explanation for returning to her family home was unreasonable and lacking in credibility.

Failure to claim in the United States - The RPD raised failure to claim elsewhere as an issue at the Appellant's hearing however failed to address the issue in its decision. At her hearing the Appellant indicated that she travelled to the United States on a visa because it took less time to obtain a visa for the United States than Canada. When asked by the RPD why she did not make an asylum claim in the United States, the Appellant said that she knew that Canada was her final destination. She also indicated that she remained in the United States for approximately six weeks while her agent made arrangements to obtain a fraudulent Canadian passport for her. The Appellant testified at her hearing before the RPD that her agent took her genuine Nigerian passport from her as soon as she arrived in the United States. She also indicated that the agent requested an additional $2,000 from her to secure a Canadian passport for her but she did not have the money. The Appellant indicated that the agent held her Nigerian passport as payment.

The Appellant traveled to the United States on XX, 2014 and remained there until August 13, 2014, when she entered Canada. She did not file an asylum claim in the United States. At her hearing before the RPD, when asked why she did not claim asylum in the United States, the Appellant indicated that her final destination was Canada. When asked how she first found out about Canada and when she decided to come to Canada, the Appellant indicated that her agent in Nigeria told her Canada was the best place for abused women.

The RAD notes that the Appellant travelled to the United States using a genuine Nigerian passport. She had a valid visa for the United States. She did not have the funds to pay the agent the additional amount he was requesting to obtain a fraudulent Canadian passport for her. The Appellant entered Canada using a fraudulent passport and did not claim refugee protection in Canada at the Canadian border. The Appellant's explanation for not claiming asylum in the United States is unreasonable. She arrived in the United States, a safe country, with genuine documents and a valid visa. She did not have the funds to obtain fraudulent documents to enter Canada. After obtaining fraudulent documents to enter Canada, she ran the risk of being detected by Canada Border Services at the port of entry and deported to Nigeria. The RAD finds it unreasonable that the Appellant left the United States where she was safe and had entered with genuine documents and entered Canada with false documents and ran the risk of being deported to Nigeria where she alleges she faced persecution or harm.

The RAD takes judicial note of the fact that the United States is a highly democratic country with an excellent human rights record, especially with respect to abused women. It would be reasonable to expect an educated person such as the Appellant to have pursued refugee protection in the United States if she feared returning to Nigeria as alleged. One would expect a person fearing persecution or harm in their home country to pursue refugee protection in a safe country they have travelled to. The Federal Court has indicated that a person fleeing persecution is expected to seek protection in the first safe place.18 As such, the RAD draws a negative inference with respect to the Appellant's allegations that she faces a serious possibility of persecution or a risk of harm in Nigeria. The RAD further finds that the Appellant's failure to claim in the United States, without a reasonable explanation, undermines her credibility.

Affidavits - The Appellant provided the RPD with an affidavit from her aunt,19 as well as an affidavit from her pastor.20 The RPD is presumed to have considered all of the evidence before it, and there is no requirement for the RPD to refer to each document in the record.21 However, where there is evidence which is contrary to its decision, the RPD must analyze that evidence and provide reasons why it does not consider it relevant or trustworthy, or why it chose to disregard it.22

In this case, the RPD simply made no reference to the affidavits, which corroborate parts of the Appellant's story and is consistent with her Basis of Claim (BoC) narrative. Neither affidavit is mentioned in the reasons. Instead, the RPD concluded that the Appellant's evidence was not credible in respect to threats of having to marry a chief.

It may be that the RPD dismissed the affidavits because it did not believe that the Appellant's boyfriend was beaten or that the Appellant would return home after initially escaping. However, as noted above, the RPD's finding, with respect to the Appellant returning home after having initially escaped, is problematic. As such, that rejection of the affidavits is equally problematic.

The Appellant asks the RAD to set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute a positive determination. The RAD is in no position to do so. There were multiple identity and credibility concerns with the Appellant's evidence and the RAD is unable to make that determination only on the basis of the RPD record and new evidence. For example, the Appellant's year of birth on her school certificate23 differs from her year of birth on her birth certificate.24 Furthermore, none of Appellant's identity documents place her in Nigeria at the time of the alleged incidents. Biometric information through the Five Country Conference High Value Data Sharing Protocol would assist in establishing the Appellant's countries of reference, an aspect of her identity, since she alleges that she obtained a visa for the United States from Nigeria and travelled to the United States in XX 2014. The RAD has not seen or questioned the Appellant and therefore cannot reach its own conclusions on all relevant aspects of her identity or credibility.
In the alternative, the Appellant asks that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination. The RAD concurs with this remedy.

This appeal is allowed and the determination of the RPD is set aside. Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel. (signed) 'M. Pettinella' M.
